selected.fullText: One Nation pushes for early super access for Australians paying rent or mortgage - ABC News Skip to main content Skip to news navigation, settings and search Explore the ABC news iview listen Loading ABC News News Home One Nation pushes for early super access for Australians paying rent or mortgage Share Share article One Nation pushes for early super access for Australians paying rent or mortgage By political reporter Holly Tregenza and Courtney Gould Topic: Superannuation Posted Mon 7 Sep 2026 at 9:27am Mon 7 Sep 2026 at 9:27am Mon 7 Sep 2026 at 9:27am , updated Mon 7 Sep 2026 at 6:35pm Mon 7 Sep 2026 at 6:35pm Mon 7 Sep 2026 at 6:35pm Pauline Hanson says the proposal will give Australians "breathing room". ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) In short: One Nation is proposing a radical change to the superannuation system that would allow Australians who rent or pay a mortgage to divert a portion of their super payments as salary for up to three years. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson says the change will give Australians who opt in "breathing room" to deal with the cost-of-living crisis. What's next? The peak super funds body says the plan is "economically disastrous" and will drive up inflation while making retirees poorer. abc.net.au/news/one-nation-pauline-hanson-rent-mortgage-super-retirement/107122814 Link copied Share Share article Pauline Hanson has insisted One Nation's proposed superannuation early access policy would have a "neutral" impact on inflation, despite warnings it would create a sugar hit for Australians while making the cost-of-living crisis worse in the long term. Under the proposal, Australians who pay rent or a mortgage would be given a choice to divert a portion of their superannuation to their take-home pay for up to three years. The full 12 per cent compulsory super contribution would still be paid by employers, but 3 per cent would be paid directly to the person by the super fund if they opted in. The payments would also remain subject to the concessional tax rate of 15 per cent, rather than the higher personal income tax rate. Are the super wars another Mediscare? A political war over superannuation has been inflamed in the past fortnight. Senator Hanson said the average full-time worker earning about $90,500 would get an extra $2,300 in their pocket each year. That works out to about $44 a week, which she said would provide "breathing room".
